q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which nuclear weapons changed warfare after 1945.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which nuclear weapons affected diplomacy during the Cold War, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity in great-power military competition between the pre-1945 and post-1945 periods.

sample_answers.a: A single nuclear bomb could destroy an entire city, so for the first time in history, great powers possessed weapons capable of annihilating each other's societies in hours — making total war potentially suicidal.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the fear of mutual destruction deterred the United States and Soviet Union from fighting each other directly, so their rivalry was channeled into proxy wars, arms races, and crises managed to avoid escalation.
sample_answers.c: Great powers continued to compete for military superiority and technological advantage, just as they had with battleships and aircraft before 1945; the arms race persisted, but the weapons being raced over became infinitely more destructive.

q1.stimulus:
Historians argue that nuclear weapons created a paradox that defined the Cold War: the most powerful weapons ever built made great-power war less likely. Before 1945, states could plausibly hope to win wars against rivals; after Hiroshima, American and Soviet leaders understood that a direct war might destroy both societies. This produced the doctrine of deterrence — each side built arsenals capable of annihilating the other in order to prevent attack. The result was a strange stability: the superpowers armed themselves to the teeth yet avoided direct combat, fighting instead through proxies in Korea, Vietnam, and Afghanistan. Nuclear weapons thus simultaneously made war unthinkable and kept the world in constant danger of it.
—Historian's account of the nuclear age in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE reason Truman gives for using the atomic bomb.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Truman presents the atomic bomb as different from previous weapons.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Truman's statement does not mention the Soviet Union.

sample_answers.a: Truman argues the bomb was used to shorten the war and save lives by forcing Japan's surrender without a costly invasion, presenting it as a military necessity.
sample_answers.b: He emphasizes that a single bomb destroyed an entire city and harnessed 'the basic power of the universe,' portraying it as a revolutionary new force rather than merely a bigger conventional bomb.
sample_answers.c: In August 1945 Truman was focused on ending the Pacific war and justifying the weapon to the American public; publicly discussing the bomb's implications for Soviet relations would have complicated the wartime alliance and raised questions about his motives.

q2.stimulus:
A short time ago an American airplane dropped one bomb on Hiroshima and destroyed its usefulness to the enemy. That bomb had more power than 20,000 tons of TNT. We have now won the battle of the laboratories as we have won the other battles. We are now prepared to obliterate more rapidly and completely every productive enterprise the Japanese have above ground in any city. If they do not now accept our terms, they may expect a rain of ruin from the air, the like of which has never been seen on this earth.
—Adapted from President Harry Truman's public statement on the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, 6 August 1945

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the photograph that conveys the power of the weapon tested.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the Trinity test changed the outcome of World War II.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the Trinity test intensified international tensions after 1945.

sample_answers.a: The fireball and towering mushroom cloud dwarf the landscape, with light and smoke on a scale no conventional explosion could produce — visually demonstrating a weapon of an entirely new order of destructiveness.
sample_answers.b: The successful test gave the United States a working atomic bomb within weeks, enabling the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki that forced Japan's surrender and ended the war without an invasion.
sample_answers.c: Soviet spies reported the test to Stalin, who ordered a crash program to build a Soviet bomb; the American nuclear monopoly was temporary, and the ensuing arms race became a central source of Cold War insecurity.

q3.stimulus: The image is a color photograph of the Trinity test, the first detonation of a nuclear weapon, conducted by the United States in the New Mexico desert on 16 July 1945. The fireball and mushroom cloud from the plutonium implosion device, equivalent to about 20,000 tons of TNT, are visible. The test's success gave the United States a working atomic bomb three weeks before Hiroshima.
